products.name: Foxtail Millet
products.tagline: The everyday millet — light, nutty, quick to cook.
products.summary: Unpolished foxtail millet from dryland farms in Rayalaseema. Cooks like rice, sits lighter, and slides into pongal, upma or a plain lunch plate without a fuss.

images.alt: A close, filled frame of raw pale grain
A cooked grain dish with vegetables, coriander and lemon in a dark pan
An open market hall with produce stacked in wooden crates

about: Foxtail millet is the one most people start with, and the one most people stay with. It behaves like rice on the stove, so nothing about your kitchen routine has to change — the same cooker, the same 1:2 ratio, the same tempering.

We stock it unpolished. That leaves the bran on, which is where most of the fibre lives, and it is why the cooked grain looks a shade duller than the machine-polished millet sold in supermarkets. That dullness is the point.
benefits: High in dietary fibre, so a plate of it stays with you longer than white rice
Naturally gluten-free — a straight swap for wheat in upma and khichdi
Low-input, rain-fed crop: it asks very little of the soil it grows in
usage: Rinse twice, soak 20 minutes, then cook 1 cup millet to 2 cups water
Swap in for rice in pongal, bisibelebath, lemon rice or plain curd rice
Toast dry for two minutes before cooking if you want a nuttier finish
products.storage: Airtight, away from direct sun. In a humid month, a couple of dried neem leaves in the jar keeps weevils out without anything else going in.

products.name: Little Millet (Samalu)
products.tagline: The small grain that behaves like fine rice.
products.summary: Fine-grained little millet, unpolished. Softer than foxtail once cooked, which makes it the easy one for children, for the elderly, and for anyone easing off white rice.

images.alt: A close, filled frame of golden whole grain
A grain and vegetable bowl photographed from above
A close, filled frame of raw pale grain

about: Samalu is the smallest of the millets we carry, and the most forgiving. It absorbs water readily and turns soft rather than separate, so it works where a firmer grain would feel like hard work.
It is the millet we suggest to households making the switch gradually — start by replacing dinner rice with samalu twice a week and let everyone get used to it before going further.
benefits: Softer cooked texture than most millets, so it suits children and elders
Good source of iron and B vitamins alongside its fibre
Gluten-free and takes on the flavour of whatever it is cooked with
usage: 1 cup millet to 2½ cups water; 3 whistles in a pressure cooker
Excellent as pongal, kheer, or a simple curd-rice base
Also grinds down into a fine batter for soft idlis
products.storage: Airtight in a cool, dark cupboard. Buy in the size you will finish in a season — unpolished grain does not keep as long as polished.

products.name: Organic Toor Dal
products.tagline: Unpolished, unoiled, and it still cooks down soft.
products.summary: Toor dal grown without synthetic inputs and left unpolished — no oil coat, no colour wash. It looks less uniform than the supermarket kind and tastes considerably more of itself.

images.alt: Metal spoons of ground spices and lentils laid out on dark slate
A simmering curry in a dark kadai, finished with fresh coriander
A jute sack spilling dark whole beans

about: Most toor dal on a shop shelf has been polished with oil or water to make it glossy and evenly coloured. Ours has not. The grains vary a little in shade, and the water you soak it in stays clear rather than turning cloudy yellow.
It takes a few minutes longer in the cooker than polished dal. Soak it while you prep everything else and you will not notice the difference.
benefits: Plant protein for an everyday vegetarian plate
No polishing agents, colourants or artificial glaze
Grown without synthetic pesticide or fertiliser inputs
usage: Soak 30 minutes, then pressure cook 1 cup dal to 3 cups water
The base for sambar, pappu, dal fry and rasam
Add turmeric and a few drops of oil to the cooker to stop it foaming over
products.storage: Airtight and dry. Unpolished pulses attract weevils faster than treated ones, so a bay leaf in the jar is worth the trouble.

products.name: Kala Chana (Black Gram)
products.tagline: Small, dark and stubbornly filling.
products.summary: Whole black chana, sorted by hand. Sprouts readily, holds its shape in a curry, and is the cheapest serious protein in the shop.

images.alt: A jute sack spilling dark whole beans
A vegetable and paneer curry in a blue bowl with basil
Metal spoons of ground spices and lentils laid out on dark slate

about: Kala chana is the pulse that survives everything — poor soil, a late monsoon, a long cupboard. It has fed this part of the country through worse years than most of us remember.
Ours is whole and unsplit, cleaned and sorted by hand rather than by machine, which is why you will not find grit in the bottom of the soaking bowl.
benefits: Dense in protein and iron for its weight
Low glycaemic load compared with refined grains
Sprouts in 24 hours, which lifts its vitamin C content sharply
usage: Soak overnight — this one genuinely needs the full night — then cook for 5–6 whistles
Sprout it: drain, tie in damp muslin, leave a day, eat raw with lemon and onion
Sundal, chana masala, or roasted as a dry snack
products.storage: Cool, dry, airtight. Whole pulses keep considerably better than split ones.

products.name: Wood-Pressed Groundnut Oil
products.tagline: Pressed slowly, in wood, at a temperature you could touch.
products.summary: Groundnut oil crushed in a traditional wooden ghani. Cloudy, strongly scented of the nut, and completely unrefined — which is exactly why it tastes of something.

images.alt: A corked glass jug of golden oil on a dark stone surface
A simmering curry in a dark kadai, finished with fresh coriander
An open market hall with produce stacked in wooden crates

about: A wooden ghani turns slowly enough that the oil never heats past about 40°C. Nothing is bleached out afterwards and nothing is deodorised back in, so what reaches the bottle still smells of roasted groundnut when you open it.
Expect sediment at the bottom of the tin. That is the unfiltered fraction of the nut, and it is a sign the oil has been left alone rather than a fault.
benefits: Retains the vitamin E and natural antioxidants that refining strips out
High smoke point — genuinely suitable for Indian deep frying
No hexane, no bleaching earth, no chemical deodorising
usage: Everyday cooking, tempering and deep frying
Warm gently and use for abhyanga, the traditional self-massage
Shake the tin before pouring so the sediment goes back into suspension
products.storage: Dark cupboard, tightly closed, away from the stove. Unrefined oil turns faster than refined — buy the size you will actually finish.

products.name: Cold-Pressed Coconut Oil
products.tagline: One ingredient. Kitchen and bathroom both.
products.summary: Virgin coconut oil pressed from sun-dried copra, unrefined and unbleached. Solid below about 24°C, which is a feature and not a defect.

images.alt: An amber dropper bottle on a wooden stand, lit through a palm-leaf shadow
A corked glass jug of golden oil on a dark stone surface
A plate of vegetables, eggs and greens on a wooden table

about: The copra is dried in the sun rather than in a kiln, then pressed without heat. Nothing else is done to it. The result smells unmistakably of fresh coconut, which refined coconut oil does not.
It sets solid in winter and melts in summer. Both states are the same oil — stand the jar in warm water if you want it liquid.
benefits: Naturally rich in medium-chain fatty acids
Doubles honestly as a hair oil, body oil and cooking fat
No refining, bleaching or deodorising at any stage
usage: Everyday South Indian cooking and tempering
Warm a spoonful and work it into the scalp an hour before washing
Use plain as a body moisturiser on damp skin after a bath
products.storage: Room temperature, lid closed. Always use a dry spoon — a single drop of water is what starts a jar going off.

products.name: Multi-Millet Atta
products.tagline: Five millets, stone-ground together.
products.summary: A blend of foxtail, little, kodo, barnyard and pearl millet, stone-ground so the flour stays cool. Rolls into a workable roti without needing wheat to hold it together.

images.alt: Three round wholegrain loaves and ears of wheat on a dark floured surface
A close, filled frame of golden whole grain
Papads and dried red chillies arranged on a banana leaf

about: Millet flours are usually blended with wheat because millet alone has no gluten and tears when you roll it. This blend gets round that with the ratio rather than with wheat — the stickier millets in it do the binding.
It is stone-ground in small batches. Stone grinding is slower and runs cooler than a steel plate mill, which matters because heat is what turns the oils in whole-grain flour rancid.
benefits: Genuinely gluten-free, with nothing added to make it behave
More fibre and minerals per roti than refined wheat atta
Five grains means a broader amino acid profile than any one of them alone
usage: Knead with hot water rather than cold — it makes the dough far easier to roll
Rest the dough 10 minutes before rolling; roll between two sheets if it fights you
Also works for dosa batter, adai and thick pancakes
products.storage: Refrigerate once opened. Whole-grain flour has the germ still in it, and the germ is what goes rancid in a warm cupboard.

products.name: Stone-Ground Whole Wheat Atta
products.tagline: The whole grain, bran and germ included.
products.summary: Organic wheat, stone-ground with nothing sieved out. Darker and coarser than mill atta, and it drinks noticeably more water when you knead it.

images.alt: A wooden spoon heaped with pale powder on a dark surface
Three round wholegrain loaves and ears of wheat on a dark floured surface
A close, filled frame of golden whole grain

about: Commercial atta is usually milled and then partly sieved, which quietly removes some of the bran to make the rotis softer and paler. Nothing is removed here, so what you buy weighs the same as the grain it came from.
Rotis made with it are darker, chew more, and stay soft for longer than you would expect — the bran holds moisture.
benefits: Full bran and germ retained, so the fibre is actually there
Ground cool on stone, which protects the wheat germ oils
Grown without synthetic pesticide or fertiliser inputs
usage: Use roughly 10% more water than you would with mill atta
Rest the dough 20 minutes — the bran needs time to soften
Rotis, parathas, poori and a decent chapati-flour bread
products.storage: Cool and airtight; refrigerate in summer. Buy monthly rather than quarterly — fresh atta is a different thing entirely.

products.name: Single-Origin Turmeric Powder
products.tagline: One farm, one harvest, ground whole.
products.summary: Turmeric from a single Rayalaseema harvest, sun-dried and ground with nothing added. Deep ochre rather than neon yellow, and it stains everything it touches.

images.alt: Whole and ground spices — turmeric, cinnamon, bay and chillies — arranged on pale wood
A simmering curry in a dark kadai, finished with fresh coriander
Metal spoons of ground spices and lentils laid out on dark slate

about: Bright yellow turmeric is usually bright because of what has been added to it. This is ground from whole dried fingers and nothing else, which is why the colour sits closer to burnt orange.
Rub a pinch between wet fingers: real turmeric stains the skin and takes a wash or two to come off. That is the simplest test there is.
benefits: Naturally occurring curcumin, undiluted by fillers
No added colourants, starch or lead chromate
Traceable to one farm and one season
usage: A quarter teaspoon in dal, sambar or any vegetable curry
Warm milk with turmeric and a crack of black pepper before bed
Mix with gram flour and curd for the classic pre-wedding ubtan
products.storage: Airtight, dark, and well away from steam. Ground spice loses its volatile oils to light faster than to time.

products.name: Hand-Pounded Garam Masala
products.tagline: Pounded, not pulverised.
products.summary: Whole spices dry-roasted and pounded in small batches. Coarser than machine-ground masala, and it smells like it was made this month — because it was.

images.alt: Metal spoons of ground spices and lentils laid out on dark slate
A vegetable curry served with flatbread beside a copper pot
Whole and ground spices — turmeric, cinnamon, bay and chillies — arranged on pale wood

about: Each spice is roasted separately, because cinnamon and cumin are ready at very different moments. They are then pounded together while still warm.
A stone pestle bruises the spice rather than shearing it, and it never heats the mix the way a high-speed blade does. The texture is uneven on purpose.
benefits: No fillers, no anti-caking agents, no rice flour bulking
Ground cool, so the aromatic oils are still in the jar and not lost as heat
Made in batches small enough to actually be fresh
usage: Add in the last two minutes of cooking, never at the start
Half a teaspoon finishes a curry for four
A pinch over a dal just before serving lifts the whole thing

specs.label: Contains
specs.value: Cinnamon, clove, cardamom, cumin, coriander, pepper, bay

products.storage: Small airtight jar, dark cupboard. Decant from the pack rather than opening a large jar daily.

products.name: Organic Jaggery Powder
products.tagline: Cane juice, boiled down and nothing else.
products.summary: Sugarcane jaggery, dried and powdered so it dissolves without the hacking and chiselling a block demands. No sulphur, no bleaching, no chemical clarifier.

images.alt: A white mug of milky tea on a wooden coaster
A jar of golden honey lit from behind, beside dried flowers
Milk being poured from a jug into a tall glass

about: Commercial jaggery is often clarified with sulphur or superphosphate to lighten its colour, because customers have been taught that pale jaggery is better jaggery. It is not. Ours is dark brown, and it is dark because nothing was used to lighten it.
Powdering it is purely practical — a block has to be broken up before it is any use, and half of it ends up as dust on the counter anyway.
benefits: Retains the iron and trace minerals that refining removes from sugar
No sulphur dioxide, no bleaching agent, no chemical clarifier
Dissolves cleanly into hot and cold liquids alike
usage: Spoon straight into coffee, tea, milk or buttermilk
Standard sweetener for payasam, chikki, pongal and sweet pongali
Substitute roughly 1:1 for sugar in most Indian sweets
products.storage: Airtight and dry. Jaggery powder pulls moisture out of the air and will cake into a solid lump if the jar is left open.

products.name: Wild Forest Honey
products.tagline: Gathered from wild combs, not from boxes.
products.summary: Raw multifloral honey collected from wild forest combs. Unheated and unfiltered beyond a coarse strain, so it crystallises in cold weather the way honest honey should.

images.alt: A jar of golden honey lit from behind, beside dried flowers
A white mug of milky tea on a wooden coaster
Dense forest canopy seen from directly above

about: Wild honey varies from season to season and comb to comb — colour, thickness and taste all move. Commercial honey is blended and heat-treated precisely to stop that from happening. We would rather you got the variation.
It will granulate in winter. Stand the jar in warm water for a few minutes and it liquefies again with nothing lost.
benefits: Raw and unpasteurised, so the natural enzymes survive
No added glucose syrup, invert sugar or thickener
Multifloral, meaning it carries the character of a whole forest rather than one crop
usage: A spoon in warm — not hot — water first thing in the morning
Drizzle over curd, fruit or a plain millet porridge
Ayurveda advises against heating honey; add it after the pan comes off the flame
products.storage: Room temperature, dry spoon only. Never refrigerate — the cold forces crystallisation and makes the jar unusable.

products.name: Kumkumadi Face Elixir
products.tagline: The classical night oil, three drops at a time.
products.summary: A saffron-led facial oil made to the classical kumkumadi method — herbs steeped in sesame oil over days rather than minutes. Deep amber, faintly medicinal, and used sparingly.

images.alt: A glass serum dropper on a wooden board beside eucalyptus leaves
An amber dropper bottle on a wooden stand, lit through a palm-leaf shadow
Skincare tubes, jars and a jade roller arranged on striped cloth

about: Kumkumadi thailam is one of the oldest cosmetic formulations still in continuous use. The herbs are decocted, then infused into sesame oil over repeated slow cycles — a process measured in days, which is most of why a genuine bottle is not cheap.
It is concentrated. Three drops covers a whole face; more than that simply sits on the skin and transfers to the pillow.
benefits: Traditionally used to even out tone and soften the look of marks
Sesame oil base carries the herbs without a synthetic emulsifier
No mineral oil, synthetic fragrance or added colour
usage: At night, on clean and slightly damp skin — never in the sun
Warm three drops between the palms, press into the face, do not rub
Patch test on the inner forearm for two days before the first full use
products.storage: Amber glass, out of sunlight, cap tight. The bottle is dark for a reason — light degrades the saffron first.

products.name: Neem & Tulsi Face Wash
products.tagline: Cleans without stripping the skin bare.
products.summary: A mild, low-foam wash built on neem and tulsi extracts with a coconut-derived cleanser. No SLS, so it lathers less than you are used to and leaves less behind.

images.alt: Natural skincare bottles and jars laid out with eucalyptus and smooth stones
Cosmetic bottles and tubes arranged on pale plinths
An open jar of cream held in an upturned palm

about: The foam most face washes produce comes from sulphates, which clean effectively and also take the skin's own oils with them. This one uses a gentler coconut-derived surfactant, so the lather is thin and the skin does not feel tight afterwards.
Neem and tulsi are here for their long domestic record with oily and blemish-prone skin, not as a marketing garnish — they are high enough in the ingredient list to be doing something.
benefits: Suits oily and combination skin without over-drying it
Free of sulphates, parabens and synthetic fragrance
Low foam means less residue and fewer rinses
usage: Morning and night on wet skin; work in gently for twenty seconds
Rinse with plain water — hot water undoes most of the point
Follow with an oil or moisturiser while the skin is still damp
products.storage: Room temperature, closed. Keep it out of the shower stream — water in the bottle shortens its life.

products.name: Bhringraj Hair Oil
products.tagline: Steeped for weeks, not stirred for minutes.
products.summary: Bhringraj, amla and curry leaf infused into cold-pressed sesame and coconut oil. Dark green, herbal, and unapologetically old-fashioned in how it smells.

images.alt: Amber glass bottles arranged on a dark surface with a copper frame
Hands tipping oil from a small amber dropper bottle
An amber dropper bottle on a wooden stand, lit through a palm-leaf shadow

about: Most hair oil on the market is mineral oil with a herbal fragrance added. This is the opposite arrangement: fresh bhringraj leaf and amla are steeped into a sesame and coconut base until the oil takes on both the colour and the smell of the herb.
That smell is strong, and it is the honest consequence of the method. It washes out.
benefits: Traditionally used to support scalp health and reduce hair fall
Cold-pressed carrier oils rather than a mineral oil base
No synthetic fragrance, colour or silicone
usage: Warm slightly, part the hair, apply along the scalp and massage five minutes
Leave in for an hour before washing, or overnight once a week
Wash out with a mild cleanser — two washes if you have left it overnight
products.storage: Cool, dark cupboard. Sediment at the bottom is settled herb, not spoilage — shake before use.

products.name: Shikakai Hair Cleanser
products.tagline: What people washed with before shampoo existed.
products.summary: Shikakai, reetha and amla, dried and ground to a powder. Mix with water, wash, rinse. It does not foam and it does not pretend to.

images.alt: Dried herbs, seeds and bark scattered across a pale surface
Natural skincare bottles and jars laid out with eucalyptus and smooth stones
Amber glass bottles arranged on a dark surface with a copper frame

about: Reetha contains natural saponins, which is what does the actual cleaning. Shikakai is mildly acidic, so it leaves the hair smooth without needing a separate conditioner. Amla is in there for the scalp.
The first two or three washes feel wrong — hair that has been on detergent shampoo takes about a fortnight to settle. Almost everyone who gives up does so in week one.
benefits: No sulphates, silicones or synthetic fragrance at all
Naturally slightly acidic, so it does not need a conditioner after it
Sold as powder, so nothing is being shipped as water
usage: Mix 2 tablespoons with warm water into a thin paste; leave 10 minutes
Work into the scalp with the fingertips, then rinse thoroughly — twice
Once or twice a week; expect a fortnight of transition from shampoo
products.storage: Airtight and completely dry. Never take a wet spoon to the jar.

products.name: Handmade Sandal & Turmeric Soap
products.tagline: Cold process, cured six weeks, cut by hand.
products.summary: A cold-process soap on a coconut and castor oil base, scented with sandalwood and coloured by the turmeric in it. Every bar is a slightly different shape.

images.alt: Handmade soap bars wrapped in paper, resting on wood beside dried lavender
Skincare tubes, jars and a jade roller arranged on striped cloth
Whole and ground spices — turmeric, cinnamon, bay and chillies — arranged on pale wood

about: Industrial soap has its glycerin extracted and sold on, because glycerin is worth more than soap is. Cold-process soap keeps it, which is why a handmade bar feels less squeaky and softens faster in a wet dish.
Six weeks of curing is what makes the bar hard enough to last. Rush it and you get a soap that dissolves in a fortnight.
benefits: Natural glycerin retained rather than stripped out and sold
No SLS, synthetic fragrance or artificial colour
Coloured entirely by the turmeric and clay already in the recipe
usage: Everyday face and body bar
Keep it on a draining dish — sitting in water is what kills a handmade bar
A bar lasts roughly four weeks in daily single use
products.storage: Dry and airy between uses. Wrapped bars keep their scent for about a year; unwrapped, rather less.

products.name: Ubtan Bath Powder
products.tagline: The pre-wedding recipe, for an ordinary Tuesday.
products.summary: Gram flour, turmeric, sandalwood and rose, ground fine. Used instead of soap or alongside it — the traditional cleanser of most Indian households before soap arrived.

images.alt: Whole and ground spices — turmeric, cinnamon, bay and chillies — arranged on pale wood
Handmade soap bars wrapped in paper, resting on wood beside dried lavender
Dried herbs, seeds and bark scattered across a pale surface

about: Ubtan is not a modern product with a heritage story attached — it genuinely predates soap in this part of the world, and the recipe has barely changed. Gram flour does the cleaning, turmeric the rest.
It exfoliates lightly as you rinse it off, which is the whole reason it is used before a wedding.
benefits: Cleans and lightly exfoliates in one step, with no detergent
No preservatives — it is dry, so it does not need any
Rinses off with plain water and leaves no film
usage: Mix 2 tablespoons with water, milk or curd into a loose paste
Apply, wait five minutes, then rinse while rubbing gently
Two or three times a week; every day is too much for most skin

specs.label: Contains
specs.value: Gram flour, turmeric, sandalwood, rose, oats

products.storage: Airtight and bone dry — keep the jar out of the bathroom itself if you can.

products.name: Classic Chyawanprash
products.tagline: Amla, ghee and forty-odd herbs, cooked down slowly.
products.summary: Chyawanprash made the long way — fresh amla cooked in ghee with a full classical herb bill, sweetened with jaggery rather than refined sugar. Tart, dark and dense.

images.alt: Spoonfuls of different dried herbs and loose teas on white marble
Milk being poured from a jug into a tall glass
A jar of golden honey lit from behind, beside dried flowers

about: The amla is cooked whole in ghee before anything else goes in, which is the step most commercial versions shorten. It is also why this tastes markedly more sour than the sweet jam-like product sold in a plastic tub.
Sweetened with jaggery. That keeps the sugar load lower than a sugar-syrup base and, more to the point, is what the classical text actually calls for.
benefits: Traditionally taken through the winter to support immunity and stamina
Amla is among the densest natural sources of vitamin C
No refined sugar, added colour or synthetic preservative
usage: One teaspoon in the morning, ideally before food
Follow with warm milk or warm water — not cold
Halve the dose for children over five; ask a practitioner for younger
products.storage: Cool and dry, dry spoon only. It does not need refrigerating and would go stiff if it were.

products.name: Amla Lehyam
products.tagline: Chyawanprash's plainer, sharper cousin.
products.summary: Just amla, jaggery, ghee and a short list of warming spices. Fewer herbs than chyawanprash, more amla by weight, and considerably more tart on the spoon.

images.alt: A jar of golden honey lit from behind, beside dried flowers
Spoonfuls of different dried herbs and loose teas on white marble
A white mug of milky tea on a wooden coaster

about: Where chyawanprash carries forty-odd herbs, this carries five. It is the version to reach for if you want the amla without the complexity, or if a long herb list is a problem for someone in the house.
Because there is less sweetener masking it, the sourness comes through properly. Most people either love it immediately or need a week.
benefits: Higher proportion of amla than a standard chyawanprash
Simple enough to check every ingredient on the label
No refined sugar, colour or preservative
usage: One teaspoon in the morning with warm water
Also taken in the evening during the change of season
Not to be taken alongside a heavy meal
products.storage: Cool, dry, dry spoon. Keep the rim clean or the lid will weld itself shut.

products.name: Ashwagandha Root Powder
products.tagline: Root only. No leaf, no stalk, no filler.
products.summary: Ashwagandha ground from the root alone, which is the part the classical texts actually specify. Earthy, slightly bitter, and best taken in warm milk at night.

images.alt: A wooden spoon heaped with pale powder on a dark surface
Dried herbs, seeds and bark scattered across a pale surface
Milk being poured from a jug into a tall glass

about: Cheap ashwagandha powder often includes leaf and stalk, because they are far cheaper per kilo than root and the powder looks identical. Ours is root, and the label says so because it can.
It is traditionally described as grounding rather than stimulating — which is why it is taken at night, not with breakfast.
benefits: Long-standing traditional use for stress resilience and sleep quality
Root-only material, with nothing bulked in
Also used as part of a post-exertion recovery routine
usage: Half a teaspoon in warm milk at night, with a little jaggery if you like
Give it three to four weeks before judging it
Not advised during pregnancy — ask a practitioner first
products.storage: Airtight, dark, dry. Powdered root loses potency to humidity faster than to age.

products.name: Triphala Churna
products.tagline: Three fruits, equal parts, ground together.
products.summary: Amla, haritaki and bibhitaki in the classical 1:1:1 ratio. The oldest and least glamorous formulation in the shop, and the one most regularly repurchased.

images.alt: Dried herbs, seeds and bark scattered across a pale surface
Spoonfuls of different dried herbs and loose teas on white marble
Whole and ground spices — turmeric, cinnamon, bay and chillies — arranged on pale wood

about: Triphala means 'three fruits', and that is the entire ingredient list. The ratio matters: the classical preparation is equal parts by weight, and cheaper blends lean on amla because it is the least expensive of the three.
It is astringent and genuinely not pleasant to taste. Nobody takes it for the flavour.
benefits: Traditionally used to support regular digestion and elimination
Also used as an eyewash in classical practice, well diluted
Equal-part formulation with no bulking agent
usage: Half a teaspoon in warm water at bedtime
Steep it for five minutes first if you want it gentler
Start low; increase only if you need to
products.storage: Airtight and dry, dark cupboard.

products.name: Moringa Leaf Powder
products.tagline: Shade-dried, so it stays actually green.
products.summary: Drumstick leaf, dried in shade rather than sun and ground fine. The colour tells you most of what you need to know — grey-green powder has been dried too hot.

images.alt: A tall glass of green smoothie with mint, beside apple, kiwi and spinach
A cup of green tea seen from above with loose leaves on a spoon
Dried herbs, seeds and bark scattered across a pale surface

about: Moringa leaf loses its chlorophyll and a good deal of its vitamin content if it is dried in direct sun or in a hot drier. Shade drying takes days longer and is the only reason this powder is the green it is.
It has a distinct green, slightly grassy taste. Most people put it in a smoothie or buttermilk rather than plain water.
benefits: Naturally high in iron, calcium and vitamin A
Shade drying preserves chlorophyll and heat-sensitive vitamins
Whole-leaf powder, not an extract
usage: A teaspoon in buttermilk, juice or a smoothie in the morning
Stir into dal or sambar after the flame is off, never during cooking
Start with half a teaspoon for the first week
products.storage: Airtight, opaque jar, out of light. Green powder fades in a clear jar on a sunny shelf within weeks.

No sugar, no instant-granule base, no flavouring

Once daily through the change of season; not indefinitely

A white mug of milky tea on a wooden coaster

about: Turmeric on its own is poorly absorbed. Black pepper changes that substantially, which is why every traditional haldi doodh recipe has pepper in it and why leaving it out to improve the taste rather defeats the purpose.
Made with the same single-origin turmeric we sell loose, so you are not getting the offcuts.
benefits: Correct turmeric-to-pepper ratio, not a token pinch
Warming spices that suit an evening drink
No sugar, milk powder or anti-caking agent
usage: One teaspoon in a cup of hot milk; simmer two minutes, do not boil hard
Sweeten with jaggery off the heat if you want it sweet
Works with plant milks too, though oat milk suits it best
